items.originalTitle: Extreme Environments Push Chips To Their Breaking Point
items.summary: Orbital data centers, military/aerospace vehicles, HPC experiments, quantum, and advanced manufacturing equipment are all putting pressure on chips to withstand extreme environments. Chips that were once qualified against a limited set of operating conditions are now being designed for environments where multiple stresses hit at once. Radiation, thermal shock, vibration, pressure, noise, and cryogenic temperatures are colliding in applications ranging from orbital data centers and defense systems to particle physics, quantum computing, and advanced manufacturing.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Researchers from the Fermilab-led SQMS Center identified material and fabrication features associated with variations in superconducting qubit performance.

“The coordinated effort led by SQMS provides a scientifically grounded guide to the material defects behind variability in superconducting device performance, moving us from observation to correlation.
Researchers from the Fermilab-led SQMS Center identified material and fabrication features associated with variations in superconducting qubit performance.

By determining which defects correlate with performance variation from one qubit to the next, researchers can target those defects through improved materials processing, fabrication techniques and surface treatments.
For SQMS, that makes the study more than a retrospective analysis of device performance.
It provides a roadmap for future work.
The study was designed to remove bias from the process, and researchers who characterized the devices did not know how the qubits had performed.
Instead, each team examined the devices, documented the features they observed and quantified those features as thoroughly as possible.
Only after the data was collected did researchers look for correlations between materials defects and variations in qubit performance.
This approach allowed an unbiased decision tree to look for features that could be linked to variations in qubit performance.”
Collectively, the findings indicate that both fabrication geometry and surface chemistry help explain the reproducibility of device performance.
Across the devices studied, differences in these three features accounted for as much as a twofold variation in performance among qubits fabricated from identical materials.
This evidence therefore points to tighter control over trench depth, sidewall angle and oxide thickness as a way to narrow that spread.
While the study identifies several materials and fabrication features strongly associated with qubit performance, researchers view these results as the beginning rather than the end of the journey.

PRESS RELEASE — D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) (“ D-Wave ”), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, and the Supply Chain Management Research Center in the Sam M.
Walton College of Business at the University of Arkansas ( SCMRC ) today announced a collaboration to explore quantum computing’s impact on complex supply chain problems.

The collaboration establishes the Quantum Supply Chain Initiative Support Fund with the SCMRC, which is intended to advance thought leadership, education and independent research focused on the application of quantum computing to supply chain management across retail, transportation and national defense.

Announced during CSCMP EDGE 2026, a leading conference and exhibition hosted by the Council of Supply Chain Management Professionals, the collaboration between D-Wave and the SCMRC will explore foundational and applied research in quantum optimization for a variety of supply chain use cases, including transportation routing, logistics network design, inventory and resource allocation, scheduling and decision-making under disruption.
“Supply chains are highly dynamic, with decision-making that can have a far-reaching impact on efficiency and costs,” said Murray Thom, vice president of quantum technology evangelism at D-Wave .

Meanwhile, a new generation of children has begun engaging with an even more potent technology: artificial intelligence.

But advocates say the most important takeaway from the efforts of parents, tech companies and regulators to find a way forward on social media safety may be to act sooner on mitigating AI's harms for kids.
Artificial intelligence can be more pervasive for kids.
Children not only see AI-generated content on social media platforms, but they can also readily communicate with AI chatbots, including some on social media apps.
Many use it for help with school and homework.
Some have formed unhealthy relationships with chatbots, and experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children's brain development.
Companies are pushing AI-powered toys for kids as young as 2.
Campaigns for social media and AI safety for kids are both playing out on legal and legislative fronts.
Individuals and states have sued tech companies over concerns around their products' safety and both state and federal lawmakers are grappling with how to regulate the tech.
Some say the biggest win from the progress on social media safety this year has been heightened awareness of online dangers for kids.

evidenceRecords.text: Since October 2023, Israel has been grappling with a mental health crisis of unprecedented scale.
Noga Dagan-Buzaglo is a researcher with the Adva Center, a think tank focusing on inequality in Israeli society.
She wrote an extensive paper about Israel's mental health system and its challenges post-October 7.
She tells DW that while the country's mental health budget did increase due to the war, it was too little, too late, as the health system faced an ongoing crisis that was not handled properly.
"The biggest challenge is convincing people to work in Israel's public mental health system, both due to lower wages in comparison to the private sector and due to an overload of work," she says.

Israel's Health Ministry has repeatedly said it has increased funding and job openings for the country's public mental health system, but staffing shortages remain, especially in peripheral regions in the far north and south.
Combat soldiers have received a special focus when it comes to Israel's mental health crisis.
